The arrows go, and the table reads as fixed

Three things you asked for, and they come out as one rule: nothing in the table looks touchable until you double-click it, and a double-click opens the thing itself rather than a box you then have to press.

Drawn 18 September 2026 From the running register, not a sketch Nothing built until you say so

What you sent

“On opening something the arrow appears, no need for the arrow. And for the roles as well no need for the arrow showing the box is a drop down box. The table in general should look everything fixed and not editable until I made the double click.”

I measured your picture before proposing anything. The row you opened stands at 60 pixels where every other row in the table is 39 — the arrow cannot fit beside the word, so it drops to a line of its own and takes the row with it.

The table when nobody is editing

Roles is the only column that draws a control at rest — a white box with a border and an arrow, on all 33 rows, whether or not anybody is changing anything. That is the thing that makes the table read as a form.

Today

Proposed

The column gives back 27 pixels and the table goes from 1382px to 1355. No other column moves, and the row height does not change.

What a double-click does

Today a drop cell takes three acts: double-click, press the box that appears, then pick. The arrow is announcing a press you have already made. If the double-click opens the list, the arrow has nothing left to say — it goes because it is pointless, not because we are hiding it.

What it costs, so you are choosing it

  1. Roles goes from one press to a double-click. That is your own rule applied to the one column that was breaking it.
  2. The … stops being pressable on a row you can edit. Nothing is lost: hovering still gives the full list, and the double-click opens a list with every role they hold already ticked.
  3. Everywhere else keeps its arrow — the Setup dropdowns, the viewer switcher, the owner pickers on a plan. Those are controls standing on their own rather than cells in a table, and you did not ask about them.
